# ChatGPT for Teens: Using the New College Planner and Flashcards to Study

> **In short:** OpenAI has announced a College Planner, flashcards and quizzes for ChatGPT for Teens. This guide shows you how to find them and use them to study one topic from start to finish. Availability may vary, so not every account may see these features yet.

OpenAI has announced a College Planner, flashcards and quizzes for ChatGPT for Teens, plus a teen advisory group to help shape the product. In this guide you'll learn to find these features, use the planner to organize college tasks, and then build a study loop: flashcards, a quiz, and a review of what you missed. It's written for students and for parents who want to help.

## Before you start
- A ChatGPT account, with the ChatGPT for Teens experience available to you. If a parent or school set up your account, some features may be limited or managed by them.
- A phone or computer with the ChatGPT app or website. The steps below work the same either way, though button positions differ.
- Your class notes on one topic, typed or copied into a document.
- We don't know for certain whether these features require a paid plan. Check the official pricing page in your account before you start.
- Plan on about 30 to 40 minutes. You already know how to start a chat and send a message, so we'll skip that.

## Step 1 — Find the College Planner
Open ChatGPT for Teens and look in the side menu or the menu icon for an option named **College Planner**. Tap it. A new conversation should open with a planning prompt or a short set of questions. If you don't see the name, look for words like "college" or "applications" in the menu, or try the app's search if it has one. If nothing appears, the feature may not have reached your account yet. Check back later, or look at OpenAI's official help pages for current availability. Once it opens, type one clear message to start.

💬 Example: "Help me make a college application timeline. I'm a [grade level] student who wants to apply to [number] schools."

You'll know it worked when the planner replies with questions or a draft timeline, and you can keep typing back and forth in the same conversation.

## Step 2 — Give the planner your real details
Good planning depends on specifics. In the same conversation, send one message listing what you know: your target start term, your deadlines if you have them, and the kinds of schools you're considering. The planner usually uses those details to shape its answer, so the more concrete you are, the more useful the plan. If you don't know a detail, say so. Don't guess. A line like "I don't know my counselor's deadline yet" helps the planner mark that item as something to confirm rather than something to trust.

💬 Example: "My deadline list so far is unknown, so mark those as to-confirm. I want to focus on [your state or region] schools and apply early in [month]."

You'll know it worked when the reply separates confirmed items from items you still need to check.

## Step 3 — Build on the plan one step at a time
A plan is most useful when you refine it. Ask for one piece at a time, such as "just the essays for the next two weeks." Each new message can refer to earlier answers because they stay in the same conversation. If the planner's answer is too long or too general, say so and ask for a shorter version with specific dates or tasks. Also copy your final plan into a notes app or document. Chat history is not a substitute for your own record.

💬 Example: "Narrow that to the next two weeks only, and make each task take under 30 minutes."

You'll know it worked when the reply is shorter, focused on specific tasks, and still builds on the earlier plan.

## Step 4 — Turn your class notes into flashcards
Now switch to studying. Flashcards are a simple tool: a question on the front, a short answer on the back. Paste your notes into a message and ask for flashcards. Look for a flashcard option in the menu if the app offers one; otherwise, asking in plain words works too. Check the cards against your notes. The AI can misread notes or invent details, so a card with an answer you can't find in your notes should be removed or fixed.

💬 Example: "Make 10 flashcards on [subject topic] from these notes. Front: a question. Back: a short answer under 15 words. Notes: [paste your notes here]."

You'll know it worked when you see 10 question-and-answer pairs, and each answer matches something in your notes.

## Step 5 — Quiz yourself and review the misses
A quiz is more active than rereading. Ask the AI to quiz you one question at a time, wait for your answer, and then say whether you were right and why. Answer honestly, even if you're unsure. When you get one wrong, ask the AI to explain it differently and to make a new flashcard for that item. Repeating this loop, flashcards, then quiz, then fixing misses, is usually more useful than one long session.

💬 Example: "Quiz me on [subject topic], one question at a time. Wait for my answer, then tell me if I'm right and explain briefly."

You'll know it worked when each question waits for your answer, and the feedback explains your mistakes instead of just saying "wrong."

## Step 6 — Verify before you rely on it
This step matters most for college planning. The AI can describe typical application steps, but it cannot see your school's calendar, a specific college's current deadlines, or any changes made after its training. Open each college's official admissions website and confirm dates and requirements yourself. Ask your school counselor about anything that affects your transcript or test plans. Use the AI for organizing and explaining, and use official sources for facts.

💬 Example: "Which items on this timeline need me to confirm dates on each college's official admissions website?"

You'll know it worked when the reply lists the items to verify, and you've checked at least one date against the official site.

## Common mistakes
- **Trusting the plan without checking dates.** Deadlines change and vary by school. Fix it by confirming every date on the official college website or with your counselor.
- **Pasting too little or too much into a single message.** A tiny note gives thin flashcards; a huge dump can blur the results. Fix it by pasting one topic or one chapter at a time.
- **Skipping the review step.** Making flashcards feels productive, but the real learning comes from answering and correcting. Fix it by doing the quiz and fixing every miss before you stop.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** A student can use the planner to break a busy week into small tasks and use flashcards to review a chemistry unit in short sessions.
- **For your business or work:** Parents and tutors can use the same loop to build practice questions from a lesson plan, then check each one against the original material.
- **If you want to go further:** Try building a full study schedule across several subjects, with a flashcard set and quiz for each, and ask the AI to rank your weakest topics for the next session.

## Try it now
Open the College Planner if you can see it, or your current chat if you can't. Paste five lines from your latest class notes and ask for three flashcards. Answer them yourself, then check each answer against your notes.
